extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent examiners and patent applicants/practitioners (biotechnology, medical diagnostics, and related fields)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing statutory subject-matter, claim clarity, and patentability of biological, medical, diagnostic, kit/package and bioinformatics inventions under the Canadian Patent Act, using purposive construction and identification of essential elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory status of higher and lower life forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower life forms (e.g., microscopic algae; unicellular fungi; bacteria; protozoa; viruses; transformed cell lines; hybridomas; embryonic, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells) are treated differently from higher life forms (e.g., animals, plants, mushrooms, fertilized eggs and totipotent stem cells). A claim directed to a higher life form per se is generally non-statutory (outside the definition of "invention" in section 2 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that are not directed to a higher life form per se but include a higher life form as a component (e.g., a composition, food product, or a use) may be statutory depending on the essential elements determined by purposive construction. If the claim is construed to be a use (e.g., use of X for animal feed) it will likely be statutory even if X is a higher life form; if construed as X or a product comprising X, it will be non-statutory. A higher life form that has been processed by significant chemical or physical modification may be construed as a manufacture. Examples: (i) claims to a plant or seed are non-statutory, whereas claims to a plant cell or a bacterial host cell transformed with a sequence are statutory; (ii) a transgenic pig claim is non-statutory, but a cell line or the use of the pig for producing odourless manure can be statutory depending on claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of organs and tissues
rubrics_metrics.description: Organs and tissues (plant or animal origin) are generally not considered manufactures or compositions of matter for the purposes of section 2 of the Patent Act. Genetically-modified organs or tissues are generally not statutory subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificial organ-like or tissue-like structures that are distinct from true tissues/organs and generated by human intervention through combination of cellular and/or inert components may be considered manufactures or compositions of matter on a case-by-case basis. Functional and anatomical differences from natural tissue/organ can indicate that an organ-like structure is statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of processes to produce life forms is independent of product statutory status
rubrics_metrics.description: A method or process may be patentable even if the product it produces is non-statutory. The patentability of a claimed process is assessed independently of whether its product is statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical consideration is the degree of human intervention embodied in the claimed process. A process that occurs essentially according to nature with no significant human intervention is not patentable. A process is patent-eligible where at least one step of human intervention is an essential element of the claim. Examples of processes considered to include significant human intervention: producing a lower life form; producing a higher life form (if beyond traditional breeding); producing an organ or tissue via genetic transformation; in vitro culturing/manipulation of cells; processes to separate cells; generating mutants using chemical/physical agents. Example: a process comprising a transformation step followed by breeding and selection was statutory because the transformation step (significant human intervention) was an essential element; the resultant plant claim could nonetheless be non-statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposive construction to identify essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment for patentability must be based on a purposive construction of the claim, not a mere literal interpretation. The essential elements identified by purposive construction determine whether a claim defines statutory subject-matter under section 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim includes multiple steps, the examiner must identify which steps are essential to the inventor's solution of the identified problem. If essential elements are limited to traditional breeding steps (which are not significant human intervention), the claim may be non-statutory even if other, non-essential steps exist in the description. Examiners should determine the problem addressed by the application and the solution as contemplated by the inventor; where necessary, focus on the solution given the greatest emphasis in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes that are non-patentable because they occur essentially according to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes that occur essentially according to nature, with no significant human intervention, are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: a claim to producing a plant solely by traditional cross-breeding techniques is not patentable even where one cross-bred plant is transgenic. If the essential claimed steps are conventional breeding, the claim will not define a statutory invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bioinformatics — biomolecules versus information
rubrics_metrics.description: Biomolecules (nucleic acids, polypeptides, proteins, peptides) are chemical compounds and claims to them are statutory. Biomolecules that express information through primary structure (sequence) are statutory as compounds. In contrast, information per se (e.g., atomic coordinates representing 3D structure) is non-statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to a polypeptide defined by its amino acid sequence is statutory. A claim to atomic coordinates of a protein (the coordinates themselves) is non-statutory because they are information. A claim to a protein comprising atomic coordinates (i.e., defining the molecule by coordinates) may be statutory. A computer model of a biomolecule that relies on structural information is not patentable (it equates to a graphical presentation of information); generic computer systems/programs merely configured to generate the model are excluded. However, the mere presence of a computer model of a biomolecule in a method (e.g., an in silico screening method) does not by itself render the method unpatentable—such a method can be statutory if the method as claimed meets other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to recorded sequences versus the information carrier
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-readable medium that merely records a sequence (e.g., sequence set forth in SEQ ID NO:1) is non-statutory because it is a carrier of information, whereas the molecule defined by the sequence is statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: (i) 'A polypeptide comprising the amino acid sequence depicted in SEQ ID NO:1' — statutory; (ii) 'A computer readable medium having recorded thereon the sequence set forth in SEQ ID NO: 1' — non-statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical and surgical methods exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A method that provides a practical therapeutic benefit to a subject (i.e., cures, prevents, or ameliorates an ailment or pathological condition, or treats a physical abnormality) is considered a method of medical treatment and is not patentable. Surgical, medical, dental and physiotherapeutic methods are non-statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain natural conditions (ageing, pregnancy, baldness, wrinkles) are not pathological, so methods to address them are not proscribed. Methods that do not involve surgery or provide a practical therapeutic benefit (for example, certain diagnostic methods, methods of treating animals for economic benefit, or cosmetic methods) may be patentable. Use claims are permitted but are scrutinized closely to ensure they do not equate to a medical or surgical method (e.g., by including a medical or surgical step).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgery and excision steps are excluded even if non-therapeutic
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that involve performing surgery on the human or animal body are excluded, whether the effect is therapeutic or not. The excision of tissue, organ, or tumour samples from the body is considered surgery and excluded regardless of reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The removal of fluids (e.g., by needle or cannula) is not of itself surgery, but a method to remove fluids may be proscribed if it otherwise involves surgery (e.g., placement of a cannula or stent) or if it lacks utility (e.g., not reproducible). Examples: a diagnostic method that requires a needle biopsy performed in vivo may be non-statutory because the biopsy is a surgical step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dosage regimes and forms — when medical element renders claim non-statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting a dosage regime or prescribed dosage amount may be directed to a method of medical treatment and thus non-statutory. By contrast, dosage forms, pharmaceutical packages or kits (physical items) are considered patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing the medical aspect of a claim (e.g., recasting as non-medical, cosmetic, diagnostic) may render it acceptable if the description adequately supports the non-medical terminology and the claim can reasonably be understood as non-therapeutic. Use claims and kit/package claims that embody dosage forms may avoid the medical-treatment exclusion if drafted appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kits and packages — definitions and claim drafting to satisfy clarity (subsection 27(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'package' is one or more components contained within conventional packaging material. A 'kit' is a specific type of package containing two or more components. When a pharmaceutical composition (a single formulated product) is a component in a kit, that unit dose is regarded as one component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be defined distinctly and explicitly in accordance with subsection 27(4) of the Patent Act; the scope must be clear to the person skilled in the art. The term 'kit' must be construed as having a minimum of two components. A subsection 27(4) defect arises where the application defines a kit as consisting of only one component or where the description fails to describe components and the examiner construes the kit as having only one component. If the description or claim unambiguously defines the kit as containing at least two components, no defect exists. Multiple independent product claims (e.g., package, kit, package containing kit) may be present if clarity is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of indefinite scope or ambiguity relating to kits/packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous or interchangeable use of 'kit' and 'package' can create a lack of clarity under subsection 27(4). A kit construed as consisting of only one component fails the clarity requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a kit claim only explicitly defines one component, the claim may still comply with subsection 27(4) if there is basis in the description for a second component (e.g., examples of possible second components). Examiners should consider whether the skilled person would understand the kit as containing at least two components in view of the description and common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions as claim components and 'kit for use' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions are information printed or displayed (e.g., how an active agent is to be administered) and may be claimed as a secondary component of a kit or package, but there is no general requirement that a kit include instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a use is defined in the preamble or body of a claim or as part of the instructions, the claim may be construed as a 'kit for use' or 'package for use' claim (e.g., 'a kit comprising A and B and instructions for using A and B to treat disease Y' or 'a kit for treating disease Y comprising A and B'). Instructions that define a medical use can make a kit novel over prior art kits lacking that use. Example: a kit comprising two formulations may be anticipated by prior art, but the same kit plus instructions for a new therapeutic use can be novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical diagnostic methods — structure and examination approach
rubrics_metrics.description: A diagnostic method outlines a sequence of steps to extract diagnostic meaning from data and will often comprise steps to (i) acquire data about an analyte (identifying, detecting, measuring presence/quantity) and (ii) analyze the significance of the acquired data (correlating presence/level to a condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine patentability of diagnostic method claims, examiners must apply purposive construction (identify problem, inventor's solution, essential elements). The guidance applies to varied claim forms including direct methods of diagnosing, prognostic or predictive methods, 'use of' claims, kits for diagnosing, device claims (e.g., microarrays), use of compounds where diagnosis informs treatment, and computer-implemented diagnostic methods. The examiner should construe the claimed subject-matter to determine whether it is a diagnostic method per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the problem for diagnostic claims: data acquisition vs data analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of the problem and solution informs purposive construction. For diagnostics, the inventor is generally solving a data acquisition problem and/or a data analysis problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators of a data acquisition problem include disclosure of a novel/non-CGK analyte, a novel/non-CGK combination of biomarkers, a novel/non-CGK means to identify or quantify an analyte, application of a CGK identification means to a non-standard sample/population, performance within specific non-standard constraints (timing), explicit statements that the problem relates to identification/quantification, detailed technical description of acquisition, and emphasis on challenges/deficiencies of prior acquisition methods. Indicators of a data analysis problem include explicit statements that the problem is data analysis, emphasis on discovery of a new correlation between a (known) analyte and a condition with little technical detail on acquiring the analyte, indication that acquisition is CGK, and lack of any explicit indication that practical acquisition problems were solved. Examiners should use these factors to determine which problem is being addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the solution to the identified diagnostic problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution is the element or set of elements essential to resolving the identified problem. For claims including solutions to more than one problem, examination should focus on one solution (guided by the description and the solution given greatest emphasis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a data acquisition problem is identified, the solution comprises elements that provide means to acquire data about the analyte. The examiner must determine which claim elements are essential to the inventor's chosen solution and perform purposive construction accordingly; if a different solution must be considered, the analysis should be redone focusing on that solution.
